questions.question: A 79-year-old man taking dabigatran presents with a 15 mL cerebellar haemorrhage and progressive drowsiness. His last dose was five hours ago and renal function is normal. Which specific reversal agent is indicated?
questions.explanation: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with far greater affinity than thrombin and produces rapid and near-complete reversal, given as two 2.5 g boluses. Prothrombin complex concentrate is the most plausible alternative and is used when idarucizumab is unavailable, but it does not remove circulating drug and reverses the anticoagulant effect less reliably. Andexanet is specific to factor Xa inhibitors, protamine reverses heparin, and recombinant factor VIIa has no established role in intracerebral haemorrhage.
options: Idarucizumab given as two consecutive 2.5 g intravenous boluses
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 50 units per kilogram
Recombinant activated factor VII with tranexamic acid cover
Andexanet alfa given as a bolus followed by a two-hour infusion
Protamine sulphate titrated against the activated clotting time

questions.question: A 66-year-old with first presentation of AECOPD has purulent sputum. Antibiotics are indicated. Which bacterial organisms are most commonly implicated in typical community-acquired AECOPD exacerbations?
questions.explanation: In typical community-acquired acute exacerbations of COPD, the three most common bacterial pathogens are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. These organisms colonise the lower airways in a significant proportion of COPD patients at baseline and are responsible for the majority of bacterial exacerbations. Antibiotic selection should be based on local resistance patterns but should cover these three organisms in uncomplicated AECOPD. The pathogen spectrum shifts in patients with recurrent exacerbations, severe airflow limitation, or those requiring mechanical ventilation, where gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas become more prevalent.
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Legionella pneumophila, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans, and Pneumocystis jirovecii
Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis
Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, and Proteus mirabilis

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with a recent history of a tick bite and an erythema migrans rash presents with dizziness and is found to have high-grade AV block. Serology confirms Lyme disease. What is the most appropriate management approach for the AV block?
questions.explanation: AV block is the most common cardiac manifestation of the myocarditis associated with Lyme disease. It frequently resolves with antibiotic treatment of the underlying infection, but may require temporary pacing while treatment takes effect. Permanent pacemaker implantation is not the default first step, since the block is often reversible; the AV block is directly related to the Lyme myocarditis rather than an incidental finding; atropine may have a symptomatic role but is not curative without treating the underlying infection; and corticosteroids are not the described definitive treatment.
options: No cardiac-specific treatment is needed; the AV block is entirely unrelated to the Lyme disease and should be investigated as a completely separate, incidental cardiac process requiring its own workup
Corticosteroids are the definitive treatment for Lyme-associated AV block
Permanent pacemaker implantation is required immediately, as Lyme-associated AV block does not resolve
Antibiotic treatment should be started, as the AV block frequently resolves with treatment of the underlying infection, though temporary pacing may be needed in the interim
Atropine alone is curative and no antimicrobial therapy is required

questions.question: The ISTH DIC score uses four laboratory parameters to assess for overt DIC. Which set of parameters is correct, and what total score threshold supports a diagnosis of overt DIC?
questions.explanation: The ISTH DIC score uses four laboratory values: platelet count (0–2 points), fibrin-related marker such as D-dimer or FDP (0–3 points), PT prolongation (0–2 points), and fibrinogen level (0–1 point), for a maximum of 8 points. A score ≥5 supports a diagnosis of overt DIC. The ISTH score has high specificity but relatively low sensitivity. ADAMTS13 is not part of the ISTH score. aPTT and antithrombin III are not components.
options: Platelet count, aPTT prolongation, antithrombin III level, and D-dimer — ISTH score ≥4 supports overt DIC
Platelet count, SOFA score, and PT-INR — SIC score ≥4 supports sepsis-induced coagulopathy
Platelet count, PT prolongation, fibrin-related marker (D-dimer/FDP), and fibrinogen level — ISTH score ≥5 supports overt DIC
Platelet count, fibrinogen, D-dimer, and ADAMTS13 activity — ISTH score ≥6 supports overt DIC
SIRS criteria, platelet count, PT ratio, and fibrin marker — JAAM score ≥5 supports overt DIC

questions.question: Regarding systemic corticosteroid therapy in acute exacerbation of COPD:
questions.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are standard therapy for AECOPD across all but the mildest severity categories and should be started within 1 hour of ED presentation. Serial studies show no benefit from tapering — stopping at 5 days is as effective as longer courses. Oral prednisolone has equivalent bioavailability and efficacy to intravenous forms and is preferred for patients who can swallow. Corticosteroids are not restricted to ventilated patients — they reduce treatment failures and shorten recovery time in hospitalised non-ventilated patients as well.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Oral prednisolone is equally effective to intravenous administration for treating AECOPD when the patient can take oral medication

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tapering corticosteroid schedule following the initial 5-day course significantly reduces relapse rates compared with stopping abruptly at day 5

statements.label: C
statements.text: Systemic corticosteroids should be administered within 1 hour of ED presentation for all but the mildest COPD exacerbations

statements.label: D
statements.text: Systemic corticosteroids should be restricted to mechanically ventilated COPD patients; they offer no benefit in non-ventilated admissions

questions.question: A patient requiring 10 days of parenteral nutrition has no central venous catheter in place. Which statement about vascular access for PN is most accurate?
questions.explanation: A peripherally inserted central catheter has its tip positioned at the cavoatrial junction, providing true central venous access despite peripheral insertion. This makes it suitable for hyperosmolar PN, and it is the preferred choice when PN is expected to last more than 6 days as it avoids repeated central line insertion, has lower infection rates than non-tunnelled CVCs in some settings, and can be managed in ward and community settings. PICC lumens are adequate for PN infusion rates. Femoral CVCs carry higher infection and thrombosis risk and are generally avoided for elective long-term access.
options: PICC lines should not be used for PN because the small lumen diameter creates unacceptable flow resistance
A peripheral cannula is adequate for any PN formulation as long as the infusion rate is kept below 60 mL/h
A non-tunnelled femoral central venous catheter is preferred for all PN lasting more than 7 days
A PICC is an appropriate vascular access for PN expected to last more than 6 days, as its tip is positioned centrally
Peripheral PN can be administered through any central catheter regardless of osmolarity, so PICC choice makes no difference

questions.question: Regarding serum protein markers used in nutritional assessment of critically ill patients:
questions.explanation: Serum albumin has a half-life of approximately 20 days — not 2 days, which belongs to transthyretin. Because of this long half-life and its sensitivity to fluid redistribution, albumin falls immediately with resuscitation and cannot indicate acute nutritional depletion. Current guidance explicitly states that serum protein levels should not be used in initial nutritional assessment of inpatients. Transthyretin has a shorter half-life (2 days) but is equally influenced by inflammation and acute stress, which limits all these proteins as reliable nutritional markers during active critical illness.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Serum albumin has a half-life of approximately 2 days, making it a sensitive indicator of acute nutritional changes

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serum albumin should be routinely used as the primary marker to guide initial nutritional assessment in ICU patients

statements.label: C
statements.text: Plasma transthyretin (prealbumin) is markedly influenced by acute stress and the inflammatory response, limiting its utility as a standalone nutritional biomarker

statements.label: D
statements.text: A falling serum albumin within 24 hours of fluid resuscitation reliably indicates acute protein depletion

questions.question: Regarding grading and diagnosis of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, evaluate each statement.
questions.explanation: The modified Fisher scale grades the volume and distribution of cisternal and ventricular blood and correlates with the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia, whereas the World Federation grade is built from the Glasgow Coma Scale score together with the presence of a major focal deficit. Computed tomography approaches complete sensitivity within the first six hours but declines steadily thereafter as blood is cleared, which is why lumbar puncture for xanthochromia retains a role in the patient presenting late with a convincing history. Relying on a negative scan at twelve hours is a recognised route to a missed sentinel bleed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The modified Fisher grade predicts the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A negative computed tomogram performed twelve hours after headache onset makes lumbar puncture unnecessary.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sensitivity of non-contrast computed tomography for subarachnoid blood falls appreciably beyond six hours from ictus.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies grade is derived from blood pressure and pupil size.

questions.question: A patient is established on CVVHDF for AKI.
questions.explanation: Convection clears larger molecules, the usual delivered target is 20-25 mL/kg/h, and clearance depends on flows and membrane. Pre-filter fluid dilutes blood entering the filter and reduces, rather than increases, clearance.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A delivered effluent dose of 20-25 mL/kg/h is the usual target

statements.label: B
statements.text: Convection can remove larger middle-molecules than diffusion alone

statements.label: C
statements.text: Clearance depends on effluent and dialysate flow and on membrane properties

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pre-filter replacement fluid increases drug clearance

questions.question: Which of the following is the most widely used clinical definition of massive transfusion in adult trauma?
questions.explanation: The most widely used definition is transfusion of ≥10 units of packed RBCs within 24 hours, which approximates the total blood volume of an average adult. Alternative definitions include ≥4 units in 1 hour with anticipated ongoing need, or 50% total blood volume replacement within 3 hours. Prediction tools (TASH, ABC score, Red Flag score) help identify likely massive transfusion candidates early.
options: Transfusion of ≥4 units of packed RBCs in 1 hour with anticipated continued need
Transfusion of ≥10 units of packed RBCs within 24 hours
Any transfusion exceeding 2 L of combined blood products in the first hour
Replacement of 100% of the estimated blood volume within 6 hours
Transfusion of ≥5 units of packed RBCs within the first 12 hours of admission

questions.question: Regarding the triage implications of therapeutic response in acute COPD versus acute asthma, which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The initial response to therapy carries fundamentally different triage implications in asthma versus COPD. In asthma, where bronchospasm is potentially rapidly reversible, failure to improve within 1–2 hours signals a severe attack and mandates a ward capable of providing NIV or intubation. In COPD, therapeutic response is typically slower, so triage relies more on ongoing severity monitoring than on early response. A COPD patient who responds well may be appropriate for a monitored general ward; one who does not should have ventilatory support available. Neither disease mandates ICU admission by default — severity trajectory and patient-specific factors determine placement.
questions.section: Part II: Initial Evaluation and Triage
options: COPD patients require ICU admission by default because therapeutic response has no bearing on triage
In asthma, failure to improve within 1–2 hours of initial treatment is a decisive triage indicator for a setting with ventilatory support capability
In COPD a rapid response within 1–2 hours means the patient can safely be observed on a general ward without monitoring for ventilatory failure
Asthma patients rarely deteriorate to respiratory arrest and may be safely observed on a general ward regardless of initial response
Both diseases respond equally rapidly to bronchodilators; triage is determined solely by arterial blood gas results

questions.question: A 42-year-old with short bowel syndrome and high-output ileostomy (2.5 L liquid stool/day) is receiving parenteral nutrition. What daily zinc dose is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Standard zinc requirements are 2.5–10 mg/day, but this must be supplemented by an additional 10 mg per litre of liquid stool output. In this patient with 2.5 L/day of high-output ileostomy, total zinc requirements are therefore at least 27.5 mg/day — substantially above standard PN dosing. Zinc depletion is common in high-output fistulae, burns, prolonged diarrhoea, and CRRT. Standard multi-trace element solutions provide baseline doses appropriate for most patients but do not account for these augmented losses.
options: 25 mg/day as a fixed high dose regardless of clinical context
2.5 mg/day (standard PN dose) without adjustment for output
Standard multi-trace element solutions in PN always provide sufficient zinc for all clinical scenarios
2.5–10 mg/day as baseline plus 10 mg per litre of liquid stool output
Zinc supplementation is only required in burn patients and those on CRRT

questions.question: Which of the following is most associated with an increased risk of extubation/weaning failure?
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] Reformulated from SBA risk-factor list. Weak cough strength and high secretion load are recognised risk factors for weaning failure, alongside positive (not negative) fluid balance, age over 65, and longer ventilation duration. Each incorrect option is the opposite of an actual risk factor.
options: Negative fluid balance
Age younger than 65
Strong cough with minimal secretions
Short duration of mechanical ventilation
Weak cough strength and a high secretion load

questions.question: At a journal club, a colleague states that ESPEN protein intake recommendations for ICU patients are based on Level A RCT evidence, with the EAT-ICU trial having established 1.5 g/kg/day as the target. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The ESPEN guidelines' recommendation on protein intake in critical illness was explicitly graded Level Zero — the lowest level — reflecting the absence of consistent strong RCT data in favour of any specific protein dosage. The EAT-ICU trial evaluated individualised up-to-target provision of protein and energy in the first week of critical illness but did not demonstrate improved survival from this approach. This underscores that while protein provision is clinically important, the optimal dose and timing remain areas of active research and uncertainty.
options: Incorrect — only burn patients have evidence-based protein targets; all other recommendations are ungraded expert opinion
Correct — the EAT-ICU trial established that individualised protein targeting to 1.5 g/kg/day significantly improved 90-day survival in all mechanically ventilated ICU patients
Correct — Level A evidence confirms that protein targets above 2.0 g/kg/day improve outcomes in unselected ICU patients
Correct — multiple large international RCTs now support 1.5 g/kg/day protein as the evidence-based target for all ventilated patients in the ICU

Incorrect — ESPEN protein intake recommendations carry Level Zero evidence, reflecting the absence of strong RCT evidence for any specific dosage; the EAT-ICU trial did not establish a universally optimal dose

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman in septic shock has received only 500 mL crystalloid before noradrenaline 0.15 mcg/kg/min is started. MAP rises from 52 to 68 mmHg. Thirty minutes later lactate has increased from 3.4 to 4.8 mmol/L and urine output is <0.2 mL/kg/hr. What is the most likely explanation for deteriorating tissue perfusion despite an apparently adequate MAP?
questions.explanation: MAP = CO × SVR. Noradrenaline increases SVR and thereby MAP, but in an underfilled patient with inadequate preload, cardiac output and actual tissue blood flow remain severely impaired. Rising lactate and oliguria confirm end-organ hypoperfusion despite a target MAP — the classic trap of treating MAP as a reliable surrogate for flow. Believing further dose escalation will restore end-organ perfusion is the near-miss here: escalating the dose increases SVR further without addressing the underlying hypovolaemia; adequate fluid resuscitation must precede or accompany vasopressor use. Direct myocardial depression via receptor downregulation, isolated mesenteric vasoconstriction with other organs preserved, and catecholamine-driven gluconeogenesis as the sole explanation for the lactate rise are all less complete or accurate explanations than the combination of inadequate preload and impaired flow described here.
options: Noradrenaline raised SVR/MAP without restoring cardiac output in an underfilled circulation, so tissue flow stays impaired
Noradrenaline-induced mesenteric vasoconstriction alone accounts for the lactate rise, with other organ perfusion preserved.
Noradrenaline has caused direct myocardial depression via β1-receptor downregulation.
The noradrenaline dose is insufficient; further dose escalation will restore end-organ perfusion.
Rising lactate reflects catecholamine-stimulated hepatic gluconeogenesis rather than tissue hypoxia.

questions.question: In haemodynamically unstable trauma patients, the sensitivity of FAST ultrasound for detecting abdominal free fluid is significantly lower than in stable patients. What approximate sensitivity does FAST achieve in the shocked patient?
questions.explanation: FAST achieves approximately 90% sensitivity and 98% specificity for abdominal free fluid in haemodynamically stable patients. In shock, sensitivity drops to approximately 62% (specificity remains ~83%). This reduced sensitivity is clinically important: a negative FAST in a shocked trauma patient does NOT exclude significant intra-abdominal haemorrhage. In this setting, the clinical decision should be guided by the overall haemodynamic response rather than FAST result alone.
options: 90% — haemodynamic shock does not affect ultrasound image acquisition
Approximately 62% — compared to ~90% in haemodynamically stable patients
80% — minor reduction due to suboptimal examination conditions
70% — equivalent to plain chest X-ray for thoracic injury detection
75% — caused by reduced organ Doppler signal in low-flow states

questions.question: Regarding the mechanisms of paroxysmal atrial tachycardia (PAT) and junctional tachycardia:
questions.explanation: The approximate breakdown of paroxysmal SVT mechanisms (around 60% AV nodal re-entry, around 30% AV re-entry via an often-concealed accessory pathway, with the remainder from increased automaticity) is correct, as is junctional tachycardia being uncommon outside of digoxin toxicity. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is specifically defined by CONSTANTLY CHANGING P wave morphology, reflecting multiple competing ectopic atrial foci — claiming it requires a constant P wave morphology describes the opposite of the actual diagnostic feature, so this statement is false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is diagnosed when the P wave morphology remains constant throughout the tachycardia.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Approximately 60% of paroxysmal SVTs result from AV nodal re-entry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Approximately 30% of paroxysmal SVTs result from AV re-entry involving an accessory pathway, which is often concealed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Junctional tachycardia is uncommon except in the context of digoxin toxicity.

questions.question: Regarding RV dysfunction in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS):
questions.explanation: Claiming increasing PEEP uniformly reduces RV afterload by recruiting collapsed alveolar vessels is false — PEEP raises RA pressure throughout the ventilatory cycle (reducing RV preload) and at higher levels compresses alveolar vessels, increasing RV afterload; its net effect on RV dysfunction is often detrimental rather than uniformly beneficial. A PaO2/FiO2 ratio under 150 mmHg being among the predictors of RV dysfunction in ARDS is true, alongside lower respiratory tract infection as the ARDS cause, driving pressure ≥18 cmH2O, and PaCO2 ≥48 mmHg. Claiming RV dysfunction occurs in under 10% of ARDS patients and is not independently associated with ICU mortality is false — it actually occurs in 22–55% of ARDS patients and is independently associated with increased mortality. Prone positioning improving both RV function and survival in severe ARDS is true — it recruits dorsal lung, improves oxygenation, and reduces hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Increasing PEEP uniformly reduces RV afterload by recruiting previously collapsed alveolar vessels

statements.label: B
statements.text: Prone positioning improves both RV function and survival in severe ARDS

statements.label: C
statements.text: RV dysfunction occurs in less than 10% of patients with ARDS and is not independently associated with ICU mortality

statements.label: D
statements.text: PaO2/FiO2 ratio <150 mmHg is among the predictors of RV dysfunction in patients with ARDS

questions.question: Regarding sepsis-induced immunoparalysis:
questions.explanation: The 24-hour shift from cytokine storm to anti-inflammatory immunoparalysis, the HLA-DR <5,000 antibodies/cell threshold for immunoparalysis, and the ferritin >4,420 ng/mL threshold identifying MALS patients who benefited from anakinra in the PROVIDE RCT are all correct. Claiming immunoparalysis occurs during the initial hyperinflammatory phase and resolves automatically with antibiotics is false: it follows the hyperinflammatory phase and does not resolve automatically — it requires sustained immune dysregulation to recover and can persist, contributing to late ICU deaths from secondary infection.
questions.section: Modulating the Immune System of the Septic Patient

statements.label: A
statements.text: Immunoparalysis predominantly occurs during the initial hyperinflammatory phase and resolves automatically once antibiotics clear the infection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The initial cytokine storm in sepsis is typically followed within 24 hours by a shift toward an anti-inflammatory state (immunoparalysis), associated with increased susceptibility to nosocomial infections.

statements.label: C
statements.text: HLA-DR expression below 5,000 antibodies/cell on circulating monocytes identifies immunoparalysis in the PROVIDE RCT framework.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the PROVIDE RCT, ferritin >4,420 ng/mL identified MALS patients who showed improved 7-day SOFA reduction with anakinra versus placebo.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with pre-existing CKD stage 3 develops AKI stage 1 during a hospital admission for pneumonia, while a 40-year-old with previously normal renal function develops AKI stage 3 during septic shock. Regarding post-discharge mortality risk, what does recent evidence suggest is the more important determinant?
questions.explanation: Recent evidence indicates that after hospital discharge, a patient's baseline renal function prior to the AKI episode is a more important determinant of death risk than the severity of the AKI itself. This does not mean AKI severity is irrelevant, but baseline function should not be discounted simply because the acute episode itself was milder.
options: Neither baseline function nor AKI severity has been shown to predict post-discharge mortality
Baseline renal function before the AKI episode matters more for post-discharge mortality risk than how severe the AKI itself was
AKI severity (stage 3) is always a stronger predictor of death than baseline renal function, regardless of context
Age is the only factor that matters; AKI severity and baseline function are both irrelevant once adjusted for age
Post-discharge mortality risk is entirely determined by whether RRT was required during the AKI episode

questions.question: A 70-year-old female with history of diabetes and CKD (stage 4) is brought to the emergency department by ambulance because of acute abdominal pain. The surgeons requested a CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast because they think she may need an urgent laparotomy. The patient is hypotensive (80/40 mmHg) and tachycardic (HR 124 b/min). At this point, which is the best course of action?
questions.explanation: The patient is critically unstable, and despite the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy, the benefit-risk balance clearly favours proceeding with the scan to diagnose and control the underlying surgical cause. Given her CKD stage 4 and age, there is a real risk she will eventually need long-term dialysis, which should be discussed with her directly. Delaying the scan to allow more resuscitation, or performing prophylactic dialysis first, risks further deterioration from the unaddressed surgical problem; although contrast media can be efficiently removed by intermittent haemodialysis, prophylactic dialysis has not been shown to reduce the incidence of contrast-induced nephropathy, likely because the renal insult has usually already occurred by the time contrast is given.
options: Delay the CT with contrast 48 hours so that there is time to perform more resuscitation
Proceed with the CT with contrast
Perform the CT with contrast, then send the patient for immediate dialysis after to remove the contrast
Perform one session of IHD as prophylaxis before the CT with contrast
Cancel the CT with contrast because it is contra-indicated in this setting as the patient is at risk for AKI

questions.question: Most modern ECLS circuits are heparin coated and engineered with biocompatible materials leading to reduced thrombogenicity. Despite these advancements however, systemic anticoagulation is still required. Anticoagulation targets include:
questions.explanation: The optimal anticoagulation strategy on ECLS is not well defined, and centres vary in practice — anti-Xa activity 0.3-0.7 IU/mL, ACT roughly twice normal, and aPTT 1.2-2.8 times normal have all been used as monitoring targets depending on local protocol.
options: All of the above
Activated clotting time (ACT) 2 times normal
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) 1.2-2.8 times normal
Anti-Xa activity 0.3-0.7 IU/ml

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised limitation of single-lead continuous ECG monitoring in the ICU?
questions.explanation: A 12-lead ECG can always be obtained in addition to — not instead of — continuous single-lead monitoring. The PACT module explicitly states that a 12-lead ECG 'should be obtained wherever possible' for definitive arrhythmia and ischaemia diagnosis. All other options are genuine, recognised limitations: single-lead monitoring may miss P waves if the axis changes, may fail to detect ischaemia in unmonitored territories, is susceptible to movement and muscle artifact, and relies on imperfect automated detection algorithms. The limitation of single-lead is spatial, not temporal — a 12-lead ECG overcomes the spatial limitation.
options: P waves may be difficult to identify if the cardiac axis changes
Automated arrhythmia detection software may lack both sensitivity and specificity
ST-segment changes in an ischaemic territory not represented by the monitored lead may be missed
A 12-lead ECG cannot be obtained in patients already connected to continuous ECG monitoring
Movement artifact and shivering can produce unreliable tracings and false arrhythmia alarms

questions.question: Regarding limitations of NAVA and titration of the NAVA level:
questions.explanation: A biphasic shape in the EAdi signal being associated with double triggering during NAVA, and titrating the NAVA level to the point where further increases produce little additional airway pressure or tidal volume, are both accurately described. The claim that NAVA function can be used with any commercially available ventilator, being a universal mode, is false — NAVA needs a dedicated catheter and is available on only one ventilator platform, not universally. The claim that the default EAdi trigger threshold is set well below the minimum recorded EAdi value is also false — the default threshold is set slightly above the minimum EAdi (about 0.5 microvolts above it), not below.

statements.label: A
statements.text: NAVA function can be used with any commercially available ventilator, being a universal mode.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A biphasic shape in the EAdi signal has been associated with double triggering during NAVA.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The default EAdi trigger threshold is set well below the minimum recorded EAdi value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One approach titrates the NAVA level to the point where further increases produce little additional airway pressure or tidal volume.

questions.question: A patient has received total parenteral nutrition for 18 days and develops rising ALT, ALP, and bilirubin. Which statement about PN-associated liver disease is most accurate?
questions.explanation: PN-associated liver disease is common — affecting more than 60% of patients after 2 or more weeks of PN. It encompasses cholestasis, hepatic steatosis, and, with long-term home PN, progressive steatohepatitis and cirrhosis. Management includes: using EN whenever feasible (enteral fat and bile acids stimulate bile flow), reviewing PN composition (excess glucose worsens steatosis; excess fat may worsen cholestasis), cycling PN rather than continuous infusion where possible, and monitoring LFTs twice weekly. PN does not need to be permanently stopped — it should be modified and reduced as EN is advanced.
options: LFT abnormalities during PN are invariably drug-related and must not be attributed to PN itself — PN composition has been demonstrated to be hepatically neutral in all clinical settings
PN-associated liver disease requires immediate permanent cessation of PN, as continuing causes irreversible cirrhosis within days
Lipid-free PN should be permanently prescribed in all patients who develop any LFT abnormality during PN to prevent cholestasis
PN-associated liver disease occurs in fewer than 5% of ICU patients even with prolonged administration
More than 60% of patients on PN for >2 weeks develop LFT abnormalities; use EN whenever feasible to stimulate bile flow and review PN composition

questions.question: Assess each of the following statements regarding nutritional timing and specific interventions in severe acute pancreatitis.
questions.explanation: The multicentre PYTHON trial showed no significant difference in infection rate (25% vs 26%) or mortality between early tube feeding within 24 hours and on-demand feeding after 72 hours. Continuous enteral infusion is preferred to reduce aspiration risk and maintain gut function. Fat has the strongest stimulatory effect on pancreatic secretion among macronutrients; a low-fat diet is therefore introduced gradually during oral refeeding. Probiotics are specifically contraindicated in severe acute pancreatitis following the PROPATRIA trial, which demonstrated increased mortality with probiotic supplementation.
questions.section: Feeding The Patient With Acute Pancreatitis

statements.label: A
statements.text: Among macronutrients, fat has the greatest stimulatory effect on pancreatic exocrine secretion — a relevant consideration when reintroducing oral diet

statements.label: B
statements.text: The PYTHON trial demonstrated that early nasojejunal tube feeding within 24 hours significantly reduces the rate of infectious complications compared with on-demand feeding after 72 hours

statements.label: C
statements.text: Postpyloric probiotic supplementation restores gut flora and reduces infectious complications in severe acute pancreatitis

statements.label: D
statements.text: Continuous enteral nutrition infusion is preferred over bolus or cyclic administration in severe acute pancreatitis

questions.question: Regarding the KDIGO diagnostic criteria for AKI:
questions.explanation: The relative creatinine rise criterion applies within 7 days, not 14, and the oliguria criterion requires a minimum of 6 hours, not 4. RRT initiation does automatically confer AKI stage 3 regardless of the biochemical values at that time.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Urine output <0.5 ml/kg/h for 4 hours is sufficient to diagnose AKI.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rise in serum creatinine of ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 µmol/l) within 48 hours meets criteria for AKI diagnosis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a patient requires RRT, AKI stage 3 is automatically assigned regardless of creatinine or urine output changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rise to ≥1.5-fold from baseline within 14 days meets criteria for AKI diagnosis.

questions.question: Lung ultrasound is a useful bedside examination for all conditions except:
questions.explanation: Lung ultrasound can give reliable information for parenchymal changes including consolidation, collapse and oedema, as well as pleural disease processes. Pulmonary emboli are not visualised with lung ultrasound.
options: Pulmonary embolus
Pleural effusion
Lobar pneumonia
Anterior pneumothorax
Atelectasis

questions.question: What does the EEG measure?
questions.explanation: The EEG measures the spatial-temporal average of synchronous post-synaptic potentials among neurons.
options: All of the above
The electrical activity of microglia
The spatial-temporal average of synchronous post-synaptic potentials among neurons
The connection between neurons and peripheral nerves
None of the above

questions.question: You plan to perform a cuff-leak test on a patient at high risk of post-extubation laryngeal oedema before extubation. What is the correct technique?
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] Reformulated from SBA scenario. The described technique requires volume assist-control ventilation at 8 mL/kg, comparing the inspiratory-expiratory tidal volume difference over 6 consecutive breaths cuff-inflated versus cuff-deflated, before returning to pressure support. A single-breath measurement, and pressure- or minute-ventilation-based comparisons, do not match this described method.
options: Switch to volume assist-control ventilation (VT 8 mL/kg); measure the difference between inspiratory and expiratory tidal volume over 6 consecutive breaths with the cuff inflated, then repeat with the cuff deflated
Switch to volume assist-control ventilation and compare minute ventilation before and after cuff deflation
Remain on pressure support ventilation and compare peak airway pressure before and after cuff deflation
Deflate the cuff and listen for an audible air leak on any ventilator mode
Measure the difference between inspiratory and expiratory tidal volume for a single breath with the cuff deflated only

questions.question: Which of the following features is NOT associated with difficult face mask ventilation?
questions.explanation: Predictors of difficult face-mask ventilation are summarised by the 'OBESE' mnemonic (Obesity, Beard, Elderly >55 years, Snorer, Edentulous) plus Modified Mallampati class 3-4, limited jaw protrusion, male gender, and prior radiotherapy to the neck. Age under 55 years is not a risk factor — it is age over 55 that predicts difficulty.
options: Modified Mallampati class 3 or 4
Obesity
Young age <55 years
Limited jaw protrusion
Male gender

questions.question: The graph below shows a typical serum concentration-time curve for an antibiotic, with three labelled regions (1, 2, 3) relative to the MIC. Which of the following statements about the graph are correct?
questions.explanation: Each area of the curve maps onto exactly one PK/PD index. The peak height above the MIC line (region 1) reflects Cmax:MIC. The shaded area under the curve above the MIC line (region 2) reflects AUC:MIC. The portion of the dosing interval during which concentration stays above the MIC (region 3) reflects T>MIC. The three indices are distinct and do not overlap. [Note: the source question offered five statements; a fifth statement restating that region 2 could correspond to both AUC:MIC and Cmax:MIC has been dropped to fit this exam's standard 4-statement K format, as it was the least clinically distinct of the five and its content is already covered by the statements above mapping region 2 to AUC:MIC (true) and ruling out Cmax:MIC (false).]

statements.label: A
statements.text: Region 2 corresponds to the AUC:MIC ratio

statements.label: B
statements.text: Region 3 corresponds to the percentage of time the free drug concentration remains above the MIC (T>MIC)

statements.label: C
statements.text: Region 1 corresponds to the Cmax:MIC ratio

statements.label: D
statements.text: Region 2 corresponds to the Cmax:MIC ratio

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the standard technique for safely extubating a patient with a normal airway in the ICU?
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] Reformulated from SBA scenario. The firing threshold for glottic closure rises during inspiration, so extubation is timed for end-inspiration (glottis fully open) to reduce trauma and laryngospasm risk — not end-expiration, which is the false statement here. The other listed steps are all genuine parts of the described standard extubation technique.
options: Time extubation for end-expiration to minimise the risk of laryngospasm
Deflate the cuff and remove the tube while applying continued suction at its tip
Position the patient upright
Aspirate the nasogastric tube
Administer 100% oxygen before extubation

questions.question: A patient established on mechanical ventilation shows the capnography waveform trend in the image over several breaths. What physiological phenomenon is represented?
questions.explanation: CO2 is a product of cellular metabolism, delivered to the lungs by pulmonary blood flow and detected by the capnograph. A rapid fall in the capnography trace over a few breaths in a patient already established on mechanical ventilation suggests a sudden reduction in pulmonary blood flow — i.e. falling cardiac output — and should prompt consideration of cardiac arrest.
options: Reduced cardiac output, e.g. cardiac arrest
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Hypoventilation
Malignant hyperthermia
Reducing cellular metabolism

questions.question: Heterogenous sepsis presentation has always been a point of interest in clinical research, under the question of 'Why do different patients behave in different ways when it comes to organ dysfunction and outcomes in sepsis?'. Based on this, choose the appropriate affirmation:
questions.explanation: Stratifying sepsis into phenotypes to correlate with prognosis and therapeutic targets is valid and may impact outcomes and resource allocation. Personalised approaches have been validated in oncology and, in critical care, in ARDS. Microorganism virulence influences host response but is not the only culprit in clinical manifestations. Adequate profiling (phenotyping) can contribute to anticipating response to support and treatment.
options: There is no potential benefit in stratifying patients based on clinical presentation and phenotypes
Every sepsis patient behaves the same in pathophysiological terms. What differs in each patient is the timing of therapy initiation
A robust rationale and evidence has been produced to address the heterogeneity in sepsis syndrome and it has shown that different presentations are explained solely by pathogen virulence
The attempt to individualise therapy based on patient genetics lacks theoretical reasoning, as it has been vastly demonstrated in ARDS patients
An adequate profiling in sepsis can contribute to better anticipate response to patient support and treatment

questions.question: A 67 year-old man with ARDS, diagnosed 24 hours ago due to bilateral pneumonia, is admitted to the ICU. PCR has shown Streptococcus pneumoniae and intravenous cefotaxime treatment has been initiated. He is ventilated with pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV) with end-inspiratory pressure of 30 cmH2O, PEEP 15 cmH2O, I:E 1:1, RR 25/min, FiO2 0.8, in the supine position. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is 65 mmHg on norepinephrine (NE) 0.15 µg/kg/min. He is adequately sedated and paralysed by muscle relaxation. Arterial blood gas reveals PaO2 9 kPa (68 mmHg), PaCO2 6 kPa (45 mmHg), pH 7.35. What is the most appropriate action to improve outcome?
questions.explanation: PaO2/FiO2 = 68/0.8 ≈ 85 mmHg, i.e. severe ARDS. Early prone positioning (sessions ≥16 h) has been shown in the PROSEVA trial to reduce mortality in patients with PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg. No ventilator mode has demonstrated superiority in ARDS. This patient is not hypercapnic and airway pressures are acceptable, so ECCO2R is not indicated. Aggressive recruitment maneuvers (peak 60/PEEP 45) have been associated with increased mortality, especially in a haemodynamically unstable patient already on norepinephrine. ECMO would be considered only if prone positioning fails or is contraindicated — premature here.
options: Put the patient in the prone position
Do a recruitment maneuver (slowly increase to peak pressure 60, PEEP 45 cmH2O, driving pressure 15 cmH2O)
Start ECCO2R
Change to volume-controlled ventilation (VCV)
Start ECMO

questions.question: A 54-year-old presents with septic shock from perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with faecal peritonitis. After initial resuscitation and IV antibiotics, what is the recommended approach to source control?
questions.explanation: The SSC 2021 guidelines recommend source control as soon as medically and logistically practical, optimally within 12 hours of sepsis recognition. Deferring beyond 48 hours significantly worsens outcomes in faecal peritonitis. Awaiting full microbiological results, which typically take 48-72 hours, before pursuing source control unnecessarily delays a time-critical intervention. Requiring emergency surgery to always precede haemodynamic resuscitation is also incorrect — resuscitation and surgery proceed concurrently rather than one strictly before the other. Deferring surgical intervention until full haemodynamic stabilisation, even if this takes 48-72 hours, and relying on antibiotics alone with source control only considered after 48 hours of deterioration, are both incorrect — source control is a cornerstone of sepsis management, not a last resort reserved for treatment failure.
options: Emergency surgery should always precede haemodynamic resuscitation to achieve the earliest possible source control
Antibiotics alone are sufficient for intraabdominal sepsis; source control should be considered only if there is clinical deterioration at 48 hours
Implement source control as soon as medically and logistically feasible, optimally within 12 hours of sepsis recognition
Source control should await full microbiological results (typically 48–72 hours) to guide the surgical approach
Defer surgical intervention until full haemodynamic stabilisation is confirmed, even if this takes 48–72 hours

questions.question: A potential organ donor's medical records reveal known HIV infection, currently on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable viral load. Which of the following is NOT an absolute contraindication to organ donation in most countries?
questions.explanation: HIV DISEASE (symptomatic AIDS) is an absolute contraindication to organ donation, but HIV INFECTION (asymptomatic or treated) is not. Inclusion of HIV-infected donors has expanded the organ pool, particularly for HIV-positive recipients. All other options listed — active haematological malignancy, TSE/CJD/vCJD, active malignancy with spread within 3 years, and primary intracerebral lymphoma — are absolute contraindications in most countries. Acceptance criteria have progressively expanded and should be verified against current national guidelines.
options: Definite or probable transmissible spongiform encephalopathy including CJD or vCJD
Primary intracerebral lymphoma
Active haematological malignancy including leukaemia, lymphoma, or myeloma
Known HIV infection in a potential donor
Any active cancer with evidence of spread outside the affected organ within the last 3 years

questions.question: Regarding the physiology of clotting and its dysregulation in disseminated intravascular coagulation, decide whether each statement is true or false.
questions.explanation: Concealment of tissue factor beneath the endothelium is the anatomical barrier that localises coagulation; its widespread exposure, or its delivery on circulating microparticles from necrotic or malignant cells, is what permits dissemination. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 does the opposite of promoting fibrinolysis — it inhibits tissue and urokinase plasminogen activators, so the raised levels seen in sepsis and late after trauma favour thrombosis. Factor VIII is synthesised by endothelium rather than hepatocytes, so theory predicts it should stay high in liver disease and fall in consumptive DIC, but in practice it does not discriminate reliably. Antithrombin III, potentiated by endothelial heparan sulfates and by pharmacological heparins, neutralises thrombin and the intrinsic factors, and its levels commonly fall in critical illness.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A high factor VIII level reliably distinguishes liver-related coagulopathy from overt DIC.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tissue factor is normally located subendothelially and concealed from circulating clotting factors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 promotes fibrinolysis and its rise in sepsis predisposes to bleeding.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Antithrombin III inactivates thrombin and also intrinsic pathway factors IXa through XIIa.

questions.question: This image was obtained during lower endoscopy in a 65-year-old man who developed profuse watery diarrhoea, fever of 38.9°C, and leucocytes 22×10⁹/L, 10 days after initiating broad-spectrum antibiotics. A PCR assay for C. difficile toxin genes was pending at the time of endoscopy. What finding is shown, and under what circumstances is endoscopy appropriate in the diagnostic workup of CDI?
questions.explanation: The endoscopic image shows raised, yellowish-white plaques on erythematous oedematous mucosa — pseudomembranes — the characteristic appearance of pseudomembranous colitis due to CDI. Endoscopy is NOT a routine first-line diagnostic investigation for CDI; laboratory diagnostics (GDH screening, toxin EIA, and NAAT/PCR) are the standard pathway. Endoscopy is appropriate when CDI is strongly suspected despite negative laboratory assay, when other diagnoses (ischaemic colitis, IBD) must be excluded, or when CDI is severe and a rapid diagnosis is needed to avoid treatment delay. Importantly, not all CDI patients have pseudomembranes — particularly those with mild, early, or partially treated disease.
options: Ischaemic colitis; endoscopy is the mandatory first-line investigation for all ICU patients with diarrhoea
CMV colitis; endoscopy should precede microbiological testing in all CDI-suspected patients
Ulcerative colitis flare requiring histological confirmation from mucosal biopsies before CDI treatment
Pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridioides difficile; endoscopy is appropriate when CDI is strongly suspected despite negative laboratory assay or when other diagnoses need exclusion

Normal colon; the yellowish plaques represent non-significant post-antibiotic mucosal inflammatory changes that resolve spontaneously without therapy and are not associated with CDI or any other pathological condition requiring treatment

questions.question: Regarding electrolyte management during nutritional support in the ICU:
questions.explanation: Serum phosphate should be monitored daily in patients receiving nutritional support, not weekly — particularly important during feeding initiation when refeeding syndrome risk is highest. The recommended minimum daily doses of phosphate >16 mmol/day and magnesium >200 mg/day are correct. Critically ill patients frequently develop electrolyte abnormalities from non-nutritional causes including organ dysfunction, fluid shifts, medications, and sepsis — attributing all abnormalities to nutrition would be an error. The dissociation between plasma and intracellular concentrations means normal plasma values can coexist with significant intracellular depletion.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Special clinical attention to early intracellular deficiencies of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium is warranted even when plasma concentrations appear within normal range

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serum phosphate levels require monitoring only weekly in stable ICU patients receiving nutritional support

statements.label: C
statements.text: Electrolyte abnormalities in all critically ill patients are attributable to nutritional deficiency and should be corrected by adjusting the nutritional prescription

statements.label: D
statements.text: Minimum daily nutritional requirements include phosphate >16 mmol/day and magnesium >200 mg/day (8.3 mmol)

questions.question: A patient with known CKD has a baseline serum creatinine of 3.9 mg/dl (345 µmol/l). Over the next 48 hours it rises by 0.3 mg/dl. According to KDIGO, how should this be staged?
questions.explanation: KDIGO stage 3 includes an absolute serum creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dl (≥354 µmol/l); even a modest 0.3 mg/dl rise crosses this absolute threshold here. The same absolute rise in a patient with normal baseline renal function would only meet stage 1 criteria — illustrating a key limitation of creatinine-based staging in patients with high baseline creatinine.
options: AKI stage 2
AKI stage 3
AKI stage 1
No AKI, since the relative rise is minimal in a patient with advanced CKD
Staging cannot be applied because the patient has pre-existing CKD

questions.question: In the case of a stable stroke patient your decisions for acute therapy will be:
questions.explanation: There is class I evidence for the use of intravenous thrombolysis when administered as soon as possible but within 4.5 hours of stroke onset. Intracranial haemorrhage must be excluded by cranial imaging prior to the administration of thrombolysis. Patients with acute basilar or large cerebellar infarctions are at high risk of neurological deterioration and should be managed in a centre with the appropriate intensive care and interventional/surgical facilities. Full-dose heparin is not indicated for all stroke subtypes. Acute CEA carries prohibitive risk in large MCA infarction.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Organise transfer of the acute stroke patient to a centre with neurosurgical and invasive neuro-radiological expertise when your diagnostic efforts reveal acute basilar stroke or large cerebellar infarction

statements.label: B
statements.text: Administration of full-dose heparin anticoagulation for every subtype of stroke and maintenance of dose for prophylaxis against recurrent stroke

statements.label: C
statements.text: Consider i.v. rtPA thrombolysis if an intracerebral haemorrhage  has been excluded by cranial CT 7.5 h after the first symptoms

statements.label: D
statements.text: Organise acute carotid endarterectomy in patients with large MCA infarction and 70% stenosis of the ipsilateral ICA

questions.question: During the acute phase of critical illness, a 58-year-old man with severe sepsis is maintained on mechanical ventilation. His family asks whether aggressive early nutrition can prevent muscle wasting. Which statement best reflects current understanding of catabolism in this setting?
questions.explanation: Catabolism in the acute phase of critical illness is driven by a neuroendocrine-cytokine response that renders tissues resistant to anabolic signals — including both insulin and exogenous nutrition. This anabolic resistance cannot be overcome by providing more nutrients and may be worsened by overfeeding. Nutritional support aims to limit, not eliminate, muscle protein loss. The nearest distractors are wrong because neither high-protein provision nor insulin alone reverses the fundamental resistance to anabolism seen during this phase.
options: Catabolism is primarily driven by inadequate caloric intake and will resolve with full enteral feeding
Muscle protein breakdown during the acute phase cannot be inhibited by nutritional support alone
Insulin administration alone is sufficient to restore anabolic signalling in critical illness
Anabolic resistance in the acute phase responds reliably to high-protein supplementation from day 1
Early parenteral nutrition has been shown to completely prevent protein loss in sepsis

questions.question: The eCASH concept (Vincent et al., 2016) describes a patient-centred philosophy for ICU comfort management. Which of the following is NOT a component of the eCASH framework as shown?
questions.explanation: eCASH (early Comfort using Analgesia, minimal Sedatives and maximum Humane care) comprises four pillars: the patient goal of Comfortable/Cooperative/Calm; opioids plus multimodal adjuvants as the analgesic strategy; sedatives minimised and titrated to a pre-specified goal with unjustified deep sedation explicitly avoided; and non-pharmacological approaches — mobilisation, sleep promotion, environmental modulation, and family engagement. Routine deep sedation is directly contrary to eCASH principles. The framework emphasises that many ventilated patients do not require sedative drugs at all.
options: Comfortable, cooperative, and calm as the primary patient goal
Sedatives minimised, targeted to a pre-specified goal, and unjustified deep sedation avoided
Routine deep sedation to prevent awareness and self-extubation in all ventilated patients
Mobilisation, sleep promotion, environmental modulation, and family engagement
Opioids and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesic adjuvants

questions.question: Which intervention represents the cornerstone of DIC management?
questions.explanation: The cornerstone of DIC management is treatment of the underlying disorder. DIC is always secondary, and if the triggering cause is eliminated — whether sepsis source control, delivery of the placenta in obstetric DIC, or antineoplastic therapy in malignancy — DIC will resolve. Supportive measures (anticoagulation, transfusion support) are adjuncts, not primary treatments. Recombinant activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa) was withdrawn from the market after the PROWESS-SHOCK trial showed no mortality benefit in sepsis.
options: Emergency platelet transfusion to maintain count above 50×10⁹/L in all DIC patients
Urgent fresh frozen plasma transfusion at a volume of 15 mL/kg to replace all consumed coagulation factors
Treatment of the underlying disorder triggering DIC — if eliminated, DIC will resolve
Immediate administration of recombinant activated protein C to restore anticoagulant balance
Therapeutic anticoagulation with full-dose unfractionated heparin to prevent macrothrombosis

questions.question: A patient with carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii VAP is started on intravenous colistin with a loading dose. What is the primary pharmacological rationale for the loading dose?
questions.explanation: Colistin is administered intravenously as the prodrug CMS; hydrolysis to active colistin takes several hours, creating a risk of prolonged subtherapeutic concentrations and delayed antimicrobial effect. A loading dose compensates for this conversion delay. While colistin activity correlates with AUC/MIC rather than T>MIC, the specific rationale for a loading dose here is the prodrug conversion pharmacokinetics, not a time-above-MIC argument. The claim that colistin has a very high volume of distribution requiring the loading dose for tissue penetration is incorrect, as is the claim that colistin is administered as the active compound with zero-order kinetics — colistin is given as the CMS prodrug, not the active compound directly. Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism is also not the rationale — colistin's relevant pharmacokinetic issue is the prodrug conversion delay, not hepatic clearance.
options: Colistin achieves maximal bactericidal effect via T>MIC and a loading dose extends the time above MIC
Colistin has a very high volume of distribution and the loading dose is needed to achieve adequate tissue penetration
Colistin undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism necessitating a compensatory loading dose
Colistin is administered as the active compound but has zero-order kinetics requiring saturation dosing
CMS requires hours to hydrolyse to active colistin; a loading dose prevents subtherapeutic levels during conversion

questions.question: Beauchamp and Childress (1979) introduced principlism as a practical framework for medical ethics. Which set of four mid-level principles forms the foundation of this approach?
questions.explanation: Beauchamp and Childress proposed four mid-level principles in Principles of Biomedical Ethics (1979): autonomy (respect for self-determination), beneficence (active promotion of the patient's good), non-maleficence (do no harm), and justice (fair distribution of benefits and burdens). These principles are derived from overlapping ethical theories and provide a practical starting point when overarching theories conflict. A key limitation is the absence of a hierarchical relationship between the principles, which limits their prescriptive power when they conflict with each other.
options: Informed consent, confidentiality, beneficence, and resource allocation
Deontology, consequentialism, virtue ethics, and contractarianism
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice
Autonomy, utility, human rights, and compassion
Veracity, fidelity, justice, and utility

questions.question: Your unit proposes a protocol for high-dose selenium supplementation (1000 µg/day) in all patients with severe sepsis, citing putative antioxidant benefits. How should this proposal be evaluated against current evidence?
questions.explanation: Standard selenium requirements in critically ill patients are 60–120 µg/day (higher than for standard home PN patients due to greater losses), with additional supplementation potentially needed in patients on CRRT. High-dose selenium trials (1000 µg/day or more) have consistently shown neither benefit nor harm in large RCTs and meta-analyses. Selenium has antioxidant properties and was studied as an immunonutrient, but RCTs have not confirmed clinical benefit at pharmacological doses. Routine administration of high-dose selenium as an immunonutrient is not recommended by current guidelines.
options: High-dose selenium is beneficial only in burn patients with extensive skin losses, not in sepsis
Selenium has no role in ICU nutrition and should not be supplemented at any dose

High-dose selenium (1000 µg/day) significantly reduces 28-day mortality in patients with severe sepsis and should be adopted, based on consistent positive results from several large randomised controlled trials
Selenium administration should always be guided by daily plasma selenium levels to avoid toxicity
High-dose selenium is not recommended routinely; large RCTs showed no mortality benefit at 1000 µg/day; standard supplementation is 60–120 µg/day

questions.question: The same patient's CRRT circuit clots on heparin anticoagulation after several hours, and the team switches to regional citrate anticoagulation in CVVHD mode, per unit protocol. Regarding monitoring in the first 6 hours after starting regional citrate anticoagulation:
questions.explanation: Systemic ionized calcium should be checked and kept within the normal range, roughly 1.1-1.2 mmol/l, to ensure adequate calcium substitution, while post-filter (circuit) ionized calcium should be checked to confirm adequate regional anticoagulation, targeting roughly 0.2-0.35 mmol/l. From 6 hours after starting citrate, and every 6 hours thereafter, total serum calcium should also be measured so the total-to-ionized calcium ratio can be calculated; a ratio rising toward 2.5, especially alongside increasing calcium substitution needs, raises suspicion of citrate accumulation. Arterial blood gas, haemoglobin and lactate are useful general ICU parameters but are not the specific tests used to monitor for citrate accumulation after starting regional citrate anticoagulation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Total serum calcium should be checked, to allow calculation of the total-to-ionized calcium ratio

statements.label: B
statements.text: Systemic (patient) ionized calcium should be checked

statements.label: C
statements.text: Arterial blood gas, haemoglobin and lactate should be checked specifically to monitor for citrate accumulation

statements.label: D
statements.text: Post-filter (circuit) ionized calcium should be checked
